question: According to official data from the Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM), nitrogen deposition in Natura 2000 sites decreased by 29 % between 2005 and 2024 and the exceedance of the critical deposition value halved1. Despite this, the official Dutch Article 17 reporting states that only 3 out of 46 unfavourable habitat types are improving.

The agricultural sector faces an unworkable gap between model-based estimates and actual practice. Farmers who invest in demonstrable emission reductions at source do not see these efforts reflected proportionally in the reports. This is due to significant local uncertainties in calculation models, the tightening of standards in the interim, and the periodic recalculation of historical data sets.
As a result, policy objectives change over time and there is no stable legal certainty for farmers. 1.

What specific shortcomings has the Commission identified in its quality control of the Dutch environmental data, in particular as regards the actual validation or updating of habitat maps, and when will the underlying European datasets be made publicly available?

How does the Commission ensure that, in the ongoing stress test under the Habitats Directive, actual emission reductions by farmers are directly reflected in the 'future prospects' for habitats, rather than the outcome being influenced by administrative changes in methodology?

How does the Commission prevent Member States from creating, through annual model recalculations, an administrative trend in which statistical corrections obscure actual ecological restoration or degradation on the ground?
National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, Monitoring nitrogen deposition in Natura 2000 sites 2026, report number 2026-0018, 2026. 1
